Project/Backlog.title: Backlog
Project/Backlog.content:
overview

Planned work, by section, and the ledger of open sorrys. A row moves to Done with the commit
that completes it. Rows were proposed in the planning phase (2026-11-19); the maintainer
approves sections for implementation (so far: J0, the nimber fields, J1a, J2a, J3, J10, R1, R2, R3, J2b, J8, J8b, J8c, J8d, J8e, J8g, J9, FF-P2); Status.md says which.

Sections: V vault content, T tooling and site, R research, L Lean, J Julia. Characteristic 2
comes first in every section.
V — Vault content

V0 — Restructure the vault. Folders by subject (proposal: Fields/, Characteristic 2/,
Prime Fields/, Extension Fields/, Linear Algebra/, Analysis/, Category Theory/,
Comparisons/, Algorithms/), a Map of Content.md, a concept-note template in
vault/templates/, by-name wikilinks.
V1 — Foundations. One note each: field; characteristic; prime field; \mathbb{F}_p as
ZMod p; finite field; order is a prime power; existence and uniqueness of \mathbb{F}_{p^n}
(GaloisField); multiplicative group is cyclic; primitive element; Frobenius; subfield lattice
↔ divisibility of n; Galois group is cyclic generated by Frobenius; trace and norm; minimal
polynomial; irreducible polynomials and counting them; Conway polynomials.
V2 — Characteristic 2 (priority). \mathbb{F}_2 and Boolean arithmetic; -1 = 1 and
addition is XOR; polynomial basis of \mathbb{F}_{2^n}; every element is a square and the
square-root map; Artin–Schreier equation x^2 + x = c and the trace criterion; normal bases;
tower fields; quadratic forms in characteristic 2 (symmetric ≠ alternating, Arf invariant);
standard fields \mathbb{F}_{2^8} (AES), \mathbb{F}_{2^{128}} (GHASH); examples worked by hand.
V3 — Categorical view. Fields have no products and no initial object; the category of finite
fields of characteristic p and embeddings (hom-sets nonempty iff m \mid n, then of size m);
\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p as a colimit; absolute Galois group \hat{\mathbb{Z}}; finite étale
algebras ↔ finite continuous \hat{\mathbb{Z}}-sets (Galois categories,
Mathlib/CategoryTheory/Galois/); Frobenius as a natural transformation; ModuleCat over
\mathbb{F}_q.
V4 — Comparisons with \mathbb{R} and \mathbb{C}. No ordering; only the trivial absolute
value; discrete topology and no limits; scalar products: no InnerProductSpace, but
bilinear/hermitian forms, isotropic vectors, failure of Gram–Schmidt, orthogonal complements
that meet the space; differentiability: formal derivative, (x^p)' = 0, Hasse derivatives
and Taylor expansion in characteristic p; Fourier analysis via additive characters
(Walsh–Hadamard in characteristic 2); what “analysis over \mathbb{F}_q” means (scope of FF-004).
V6 — Nimbers and Conway polynomials: nim-addition and nim-multiplication; the nimber fields
\mathbb{F}_{2^{2^k}} and the quadratic closure; Conway polynomials and their compatibility as a
functor on the divisibility poset; pseudo-Conway polynomials; changes of representation as
linear maps. Lean: CombinatorialGames’ Nimber (check what it proves before relying on it).
V7 — Learners over finite fields (the maintainer’s experiment): what replaces gradients
(discrete optimisation, interpolation, Reed–Muller, learning parity with noise), once the
maintainer has written the ideas down.
V5 — Linear algebra over \mathbb{F}_q (was FF-003): counting subspaces, GL_n(\mathbb{F}_q)
order, rank, solving; specification before code.

T — Tooling and site

T1 — Snippet sync tool. Takes a declaration name, asks Lean (against the pinned mathlib)
for signature, docstring and module, and writes a > [!mathlib] callout between markers
(…) with a link to the mathlib docs and an attribution line
(mathlib is Apache-2.0). Plain Markdown, so Obsidian and Quartz both render it; a re-run refreshes
it; a renamed declaration fails loudly. The same tool syncs our own Lean and Julia snippets from
anchors in the sources. Caveat: the hosted mathlib docs follow master, not our pin. A Quartz
plugin would not render in Obsidian, hence the generator.
T2 — Lean API docs with doc-gen4 (the tool behind mathlib’s docs), published under a subpath
(e.g. <site>/lean/) beside the vault, as Lenticulum.jl publishes Documenter under api/;
Julia API docs (Documenter) likewise under <site>/julia/. First check whether doc-gen4 can be
limited to our modules: by default it documents every import, i.e. much of mathlib.
T3 — Note checker (Lenticulum’s check_notes.py as model): dangling wikilinks, missing tag
lines, missing sources, unlisted sorrys.
T4 — CI, remaining: a benchmark job (on demand, not per push) once bench/ exists; a job
that fails on an unlisted sorry (with T3).
T7 — Register FiniteFieldArithmetic.jl in the General registry
(subdir=julia/FiniteFieldArithmetic.jl) once it exists and has a first release.

L — Lean

L0 — Library layout under lean/FiniteFields/ mirroring the vault subjects; one file per
subject, each linked from its notes.
L1 — Characteristic 2: statements for V2 (squares, Artin–Schreier trace criterion,
CharTwo lemmas), reusing Mathlib/Algebra/CharP/Two.lean and FieldTheory/Finite/*.
L2 — Categorical statements for V3, beside the classical ones.
L3 — Generalisation survey: list mathlib results stated only for \mathbb{R}, \mathbb{C}
or RCLike that hold over any field, then restate them generically.
L4 — Proof sweep: discharge the sorry ledger.

R — Research

R3 — Lean: tower digits = binary digits (DiMuro’s Lemma 1.1) (approved 2026-11-21: “lean
proof approved! Add it to the backlog.”). The one unformalized link between the R1 data (ranks
computed with tower digits: monomials in the \chi_r times finite nimber bits) and
nimSum_lt_of_rank_lt (binary digits). On CombinatorialGames’ Nimber:

one step: CombinatorialGames’ IsRing.eval_eq_of_lt already says that for a ring x with
X ^ n ≤ leastNoRoots x and p of degree < n with coefficients < x, the nim value
p(x) is the ordinal oeval x p = [x^{n-1} a_{n-1} + \dots + a_0] (this is Lemma 1.1);
nesting: iterate it over a tower g_1 < \dots < g_k to get the ordinal of
\sum_e g_k^{e_k} \cdots g_1^{e_1} c_e, and prove that the ordinal order on such elements is
lexicographic in (monomial, then c_e), i.e. that the colex order on tower digits equals
digits_strictMono’s order on binary digits (a statement about ordinal arithmetic:
Cantor normal form base x versus base 2);
conclude: for a finite subfield given in a tower, the reduced echelon basis for tower digits
is the one for binary digits, so nimSum_lt_of_rank_lt applies to the R1 ranks.
Hypotheses of step 1 for a concrete x (that x is a field and the degree of
leastNoRoots x) are inputs here, not proved: for x = \omega that is exactly the
proof_wanted leastNoRoots_omega0 (\omega^3 = 2) of CombinatorialGames. Proving the
concrete relations (Theorem 3.1, Lenstra’s \alpha_u, R1’s 17 new values) is a separate, much
larger task, not part of R3 (not approved).



J — Julia (FiniteFieldArithmetic.jl)


J10 — Rank-encoded fields, remaining (approved 2026-11-21; the type is done, see Done):
faster minimal_degree/hash (Frobenius-power byte tables per maximal divisor; now 1.7 µs at
n = 126); bulk operations (MulBy, matrix products, bitsliced vectors) for Nim, converting
once at the boundary; embed between Nim and the Conway fields (now possible canonically:
the Conway generator is an element of \mathbf{On}_2).


J1a — Representations, remaining (approved 2026-11-21; first part done, see Done):
nimbers for n = 2^k, Conway polynomials for every n (pseudo-Conway beyond the tables),
standard polynomials (AES, GHASH, …); selected by a type parameter; conversion maps between
them. Decided (2026-11-19): nimbers default, Conway secondary, the others alternatives.
Printing always hex; the REPL adds the field when it does not fill its storage. Open:

pseudo-Conway polynomials for the degrees missing from Lübeck’s table (n = 128 and 14
others below it), compatible with the table; not canonical, so the construction needs the
maintainer’s choice;
isomorphisms between AES/GHASH and the Conway fields (there are n; which one, or all);
Conway → Conway embeddings by byte tables per pair (now 335 ns – 1.5 µs per element,
the nimber isomorphisms 0.2–1.9 ns);
table strategies for small Conway fields (products 2.9 ns against 0.4 for nimber
GF(256); inverses 14 ns with Itoh–Tsujii against 0.3);
bulk operations (MulBy, matrix products) for PolyElement;
whether Conway fields of different degrees should promote (and compare equal) through
embed, as nimbers do; that needs hash through the smallest subfield (J9b).



J1b — Arbitrary n: a function (or macro, if a function cannot give type stability) that
constructs \mathbb{F}_{2^n} for any n: picks the smallest fitting UInt for n \le 128,
multi-word storage above; finds an irreducible polynomial (low-weight trinomial or pentanomial
search with an irreducibility test) or takes a Conway polynomial from a table.


J2 — Multiplication strategies, selected by dispatch and compared by benchmark; both table
and computed variants where possible (maintainer, 2026-11-19), small fields probably tables
only: shift-and-add, log/antilog tables (small n), carry-less multiplication (x86 PCLMULQDQ, ARM PMULL via LLVM
intrinsics), reduction for sparse polynomials; profiled.


J3 — Inversion and division, remaining (approved 2026-11-21; strategies done, see
Done): division without a separate inverse (Euclid started at s_1 = x gives x/y
directly; / is still x * inv(y)); a faster Euclid (branch-free, or several quotient bits
per step); bulk inversion (Montgomery’s trick: 3(k-1) products and one inverse for k
elements).


J4 — \mathbb{F}_p in the smallest fitting UInt; Barrett/Montgomery as options.


J5 — \mathbb{F}_{p^n} generic.


J6 — Constant time: not a goal. Document which strategies happen to be constant-time; do not
engineer for it.


J8b — Bulk, remaining (after J8; approved 2026-11-20; packing, the cache-blocking
measurement, the bitsliced matrix product and bitsliced vectors at every level done, see
Done): ARM PMULL; GPU kernels (needs a GPU to test).


J8f — Fewer carry-less products in CLMulMatMul (proposed 2026-11-20, not approved): the
matrix product is bound by PCLMULQDQ throughput, not by the caches (src/bulk.md, “Larger
sizes and cache blocking”). Two terms per 64-bit product at GF(2^16) (a_1 + a_2x^{32} times
b_2 + b_1x^{32}); VPCLMULQDQ (four products per AVX-512 instruction) at every level.
Tests and benchmark first, as usual.


J7 — \overline{\mathbb{F}}_2 ("n = \infty"): every element lives in some finite
\mathbb{F}_{2^n}, so elements carry their degree and an operation embeds both operands into
\mathbb{F}_{2^{\operatorname{lcm}(m,n)}} through Conway polynomials (pseudo-Conway beyond the
tables). Exact, not fast; sizes grow with the lcm. The nimber quadratic closure (all
2^{2^k}) is the cheap special case. After J1–J3. Lean counterpart:
AlgebraicClosure (ZMod 2).


J9b — Smallest field for the Conway representation and the others (requested by the
maintainer 2026-11-20, to be implemented with or after J1a/J1b; \overline{\mathbb{F}}_2 after
J7; the nimber part, J9, is done): for an element x of a Conway field \mathbb{F}_{2^k} (any
k, not only powers of two), the caller can ask for either

the integer minimal_degree(x) = d = [\mathbb{F}_2(x) : \mathbb{F}_2], the smallest
d \mid k with x^{2^d} = x (type-stable), or
the smallest containing field type: reduce_field(x), x as an element of the Conway
field \mathbb{F}_{2^d} (its type depends on the value, so type-unstable as for nimbers),
through the Conway compatibility: x is written in powers of
\beta = \alpha_k^{(2^k-1)/(2^d-1)}, which the compatibility of Conway polynomials identifies
with the generator \alpha_d of \mathbb{F}_{2^d}.

minimal_level has no Conway counterpart unless k is a power of two. The divisors of k can
be tried from the smallest (or the largest proper ones ruled out first); measure which.
Tests first, with the Frobenius oracle of test/subfield.jl; for k = 2^j, also cross-checked
against the nimber results through the isomorphism of J1a.

Project/Decisions/ADR-0001-Use-MathStruc.title: ADR-0001 Use MathStruct Quartz
Project/Decisions/ADR-0001-Use-MathStruc.content:
ADR-0001: Use MathStruct Quartz
Status: accepted
Context
The project needs a browsable Obsidian vault with mathematical documentation and TikZ diagrams.
Decision
Build the vault with MathStruct/quartz, pinned to
6c85c0950ac0bd9567d2509dd1d50d38e4e6696c. Its MathStruct preset supplies TikZ and Typst/LaTeX
support as well as Obsidian-oriented plugins. The wrapper in site/build.sh fetches that exact
commit.
Consequences

Site builds are reproducible against a known Quartz revision.
Updating Quartz is an explicit change to the pin and should be tested against the vault.
The upstream checkout and generated site are disposable build outputs, not project sources.

Project/Decisions/ADR-0002-Reuse-mathlib.title: ADR-0002 Reuse mathlib
Project/Decisions/ADR-0002-Reuse-mathlib.content:
ADR-0002: Reuse mathlib
Status: accepted
Context
Lean is intended to state and prove the project’s mathematics, but finite-field constructions and
theorems may already exist in mathlib.
Decision
Search mathlib before adding a definition or proof. For prime fields, use ZMod p and its Field
instance from Mathlib.Algebra.Field.ZMod. New project-specific results should be proved using
those existing structures and should link to the relevant specification.
Consequences
The Lean starter depends on mathlib at the same release as its pinned Lean toolchain. Any new
formalization should say whether it is new or a direct reuse of a mathlib declaration.

Project/Decisions/ADR-0003-Keep-Julia-an.content:
ADR-0003: Keep Julia and Lean in one repository
Status: accepted
Context
Julia is the executable library and Lean is its formal specification/proof environment. Splitting
them would make it harder to keep mathematical requirements, implementations, and proofs aligned.
Decision
Keep the Julia package, Lean project, and specification vault together. Link related artifacts
from their specifications and track work that spans components as one backlog item.
Consequences
Julia dependencies and Lean dependencies remain independently managed. The Nix development shell
provides their toolchains without replacing their native project manifests.

Project/Decisions/ADR-0004-Nimbers-as-th.content:
design characteristic-2

Status: accepted (2026-11-19, maintainer); the part “Conway polynomials … the default for every other n” is superseded by ADR-0005 Rank encoding of GF(2^n) in Conway’s On2 (2026-11-21).
Elements of \mathbb{F}_{2^{2^k}} are nimbers by
default; Conway polynomials are the secondary representation and the default for every other
n; the cryptographers’ polynomials (AES, GHASH, …) are alternatives for cryptanalysis and
interoperability.


Code: julia/FiniteFieldArithmetic.jl/src/nimber.jl (and its note nimber.md).
Backlog: J1a, J1b, J7, V6.

Context
A field \mathbb{F}_{2^n} has many concrete representations, one per choice of basis; the usual
one is a polynomial basis modulo an irreducible polynomial of degree n. The maintainer asked
for the choice that gives the most structure, especially across several fields, rather than a
polynomial picked by cryptographers for cheap reduction. The project’s purpose (general theory,
cryptanalysis, learners built on finite fields) favours structure and bulk arithmetic over
interoperability.
Options considered

Conway polynomials C_n, for every n: the lexicographically least monic primitive
polynomial of degree n over \mathbb{F}_2 compatible with C_m for all m \mid n, i.e.
C_m(x^{(2^n-1)/(2^m-1)}) \equiv 0 \pmod{C_n}. Then the embeddings
\mathbb{F}_{2^m} \hookrightarrow \mathbb{F}_{2^n}, \alpha_m \mapsto \alpha_n^{(2^n-1)/(2^m-1)},
commute. Categorically: finite fields of characteristic 2 have m embeddings
\mathbb{F}_{2^m} \to \mathbb{F}_{2^n} when m \mid n (one per Galois automorphism); Conway
polynomials choose one coherently, a functor from the divisibility poset (\mathbb{N}_{>0}, \mid)
into fields whose colimit is a concrete \overline{\mathbb{F}}_2. Since \alpha_n is primitive,
discrete logarithms are compatible as well. Costs: “least” is a convention (the compatibility is
the structure); the tables (Lübeck) end at some degree, beyond which pseudo-Conway polynomials
(compatible, not minimal) must be computed; they are dense, so reduction is slower than with a
trinomial.
Nimbers (Conway, On Numbers and Games, ch. 6), for n = 2^k: the integers below
2^{2^k} with XOR and nim-multiplication form \mathbb{F}_{2^{2^k}}, and these fields are
nested as sets of integers. The embedding keeps the bit pattern; no polynomial is chosen at all
(each level is the Artin–Schreier extension by a root of X^2 + X + F/2 of the one below). The
union is the quadratic closure of \mathbb{F}_2, and levels 3–7 are exactly the byte-sized
fields of 8–128 bits, the maintainer’s priority. Lean: the
CombinatorialGames project defines Nimber
(on our toolchain v4.36.0); mathlib v4.36.0 has neither nimbers nor Conway polynomials.
Cost: no hardware instruction like carry-less multiplication helps; the large levels must be
benchmarked against polynomial bases.
Standard low-weight polynomials (AES x^8+x^4+x^3+x+1, GHASH x^{128}+x^7+x^2+x+1):
fast reduction and interoperability with existing software; no structure across fields.

Decision
Nimbers for n = 2^k, Conway polynomials (pseudo-Conway beyond the tables) for other n and
for \overline{\mathbb{F}}_2, standard polynomials as alternatives. A change of representation is
an \mathbb{F}_2-linear map (an n \times n bit matrix), cheap in bulk.
Consequences

Subfield arithmetic is free in the nimber representation: GF(16) values are GF(256) values,
so mixed-level arithmetic is promotion, and one set of GF(256) tables serves every level up to
it (measured: nimber.md).
Conversions between representations must be explicit (no implicit isomorphism); elements of
different representations compare unequal.
Fields that are not of the form 2^{2^k} (e.g. \mathbb{F}_{2^7}) wait for the Conway
representation (J1b).

Project/Decisions/ADR-0005-Rank-encoding.title: ADR-0005 Rank encoding of GF(2^n) in Conway's On2
Project/Decisions/ADR-0005-Rank-encoding.content:
design characteristic-2 categorical

Status: accepted (2026-11-21, maintainer: “Approve ADR-0005 and R1”). Every field
\mathbb{F}_{2^n} is represented canonically as the subfield of Conway’s \mathbf{On}_2 (the
nimbers on all ordinals) with 2^n elements, each element encoded by its rank in ordinal
order within that subfield. For n = 2^k this is exactly the existing Nimber type.
Supersedes the part of ADR-0004 Nimbers as the default representation of GF(2^n) that made
Conway polynomials the default for other n.


Research: Canonical extension of the nimbers. Backlog: R1 (the data), then a library type.

Context
ADR-0004 made nimbers the default for n = 2^k and Conway polynomials the default otherwise.
J1a implemented Conway fields and showed the costs: Lübeck’s table has gaps (no C_{128}),
pseudo-Conway polynomials would need a non-canonical construction, and the isomorphisms between
nimber and Conway fields needed a root convention chosen by us. The maintainer asked for a
structure that extends the nimbers to every n without arbitrary choices, even reproducible
ones (StandardFF was rejected for its pseudo-random polynomial searches).
Options considered

Conway polynomials (ADR-0004): canonical by a lexicographic rule, but tabulated, with gaps,
not extending the nimbers (a separate representation joined by a chosen isomorphism).
StandardFF (Lübeck 2023): extends the nimbers exactly on 2^k and covers every n, but
picks the odd-prime steps by deterministic pseudo-random searches. Rejected.
Conway’s \mathbf{On}_2 below \omega^{\omega^\omega} with the rank encoding: every
choice is forced by the mex definition of nim-multiplication (the same definition that gives
the finite nimbers); every finite field is a subfield, embeddings are inclusions; numbering
the elements of \mathbb{F}_{2^n} by ordinal rank is \mathbb{F}_2-linear and gives n bits.

Decision
Option 3. The element of \mathbb{F}_{2^n} with rank k is the k-th smallest ordinal (from 0)
among the 2^n elements of the subfield of \mathbf{On}_2 of that order; it is stored as the
integer k in the smallest fitting unsigned type and printed in hexadecimal, as nimbers are.
Consequences

Nimber is unchanged: for n = 2^k the subfield is the initial segment, rank = value.
Embeddings \mathbb{F}_{2^m} \hookrightarrow \mathbb{F}_{2^n} (m \mid n) are canonical (the
inclusions in \mathbf{On}_2), compatible, and fixed bit matrices in rank coordinates;
equality across fields can be defined through them.
The runtime needs, per n, a change of basis between rank coordinates and an internal basis
for fast products (any basis: it does not leak), and the embedding matrices. These are computed
once (R1) from \mathbf{On}_2, which needs Lenstra’s elements \alpha_u for every prime
u \le 128; 17 of them were not known before R1.
Conway fields (J1a), AES and GHASH remain as alternative representations; embed connects
them to the default through the canonical embeddings, which replaces J1a’s root convention.
The data are derived, so they are checked: against Lenstra’s table, against the nimbers for
n = 2^k, by the field axioms, and by the compatibility of all embeddings.

Project/Lean-and-mathlib.title: Lean and mathlib
Project/Lean-and-mathlib.content:
Lean files live under lean/; lean/lean-toolchain and the mathlib release in lakefile.lean
are intentionally aligned, and so is every other Lean dependency (below).
Reuse-first checklist

Search mathlib by mathematical name and relevant types before defining anything.
If the definition or theorem exists, import the narrowest suitable module and use it directly.
Record the module and declaration in the specification or this page.
If mathlib does not have it but another Lean library does, use that library (maintainer,
2026-11-21: “If the proof is not in mathlib but some other lean library use it!“): add it as a
require pinned to a commit on our toolchain that builds against our mathlib tag.
Add a new definition only when the project’s intended notion differs or no library has a suitable
one. State that distinction and prove project-specific properties in Lean.

Other Lean libraries in use

CombinatorialGames (github.com/vihdzp/combinatorial-games), commit 061f2c9 (2026-11-18,
the last one on Lean v4.36.0; it pins mathlib master at 285667a, 105 commits after our tag
v4.36.0, and builds against the tag unchanged, checked 2026-11-21). Used for Nimber (nim
arithmetic on all ordinals) and the simplest extension theorems
(Nimber.IsGroup.two_opow, IsGroup.add_eq_of_lt, IsGroup.sum_lt, Nimber.two_opow_log_add)
in lean/FiniteFields/NimberDigits.lean. No cache: lake builds the imported files (about 20 s).
Move this pin together with the toolchain and mathlib.

For the first specification, mathlib provides ZMod p and its field instance in
Mathlib.Algebra.Field.ZMod; lean/FiniteFields.lean checks that the instance is available for
prime p.
What mathlib v4.36.0 has (checked 2026-11-19)

Mathlib/Algebra/Field/ZMod.lean: the Field (ZMod p) instance.
Mathlib/FieldTheory/Finite/GaloisField.lean: GaloisField p n, the splitting field of
X^{p^n} - X; GaloisField.card, GaloisField.finrank, FiniteField.algEquivGaloisField.
Mathlib/FieldTheory/Finite/Basic.lean: FiniteField.frobeniusAlgHom, frobeniusAlgEquiv;
Mathlib/FieldTheory/Finite/Trace.lean.
Mathlib/Algebra/CharP/Two.lean: CharTwo.two_eq_zero, CharTwo.neg_one_eq_one, …
Mathlib/Algebra/Polynomial/HasseDeriv.lean: Hasse derivatives.
Mathlib/CategoryTheory/Galois/: Galois categories and fundamental groups.
InnerProductSpace requires [RCLike 𝕜], so it does not apply over a finite field: scalar
products over \mathbb{F}_q are bilinear and quadratic forms (LinearMap.BilinForm,
QuadraticForm).
Not in mathlib: a category of fields (FieldCat; a full subcategory of CommRingCat if
needed), nimbers, Conway polynomials. Nimbers are formalized in the
CombinatorialGames project (same toolchain).

Upstreaming a generalisation to mathlib is decided case by case (maintainer): review takes
time and may ask for a restatement; anything with sorry cannot go; until our pin moves past
the merge, the two copies coexist.
The Julia implementation is not itself a proof. Its tests check executable behavior; Lean proves
theorems about the corresponding mathlib structures. A future bridge between Julia code and Lean
requires an explicit design decision and is not implied by this starter.

Project/Problems.title: Problems
Project/Problems.content:
Record each discovered defect with an identifier, a minimal
reproduction, expected and actual behavior, and links to the affected specification and code.
Do not use this log as a substitute for feature planning; planned work belongs in
the backlog.
FF-P1 — CLMul at GF(2^64) loses its speed in the element wrapper (open, 2026-11-19)

Where: julia/FiniteFieldArithmetic.jl/src/nimber_fast.jl, nim_mul_bits(::CLMul, …, Val(6))
and mul(CLMul(), a::GF2_64, b::GF2_64); measurements in src/nimber_fast.md.
Reproduction: broadcast over 4096 random pairs, in one process. On UInt64 bit patterns,
nim_mul_bits(CLMul(), x, y, Val(6)) takes 10.4–11.7 ns per product against 18–20 ns for
MulTable. Wrapped as GF2_64 (mul(CLMul(), a, b) or
unsafe_frombits(GF2_64, nim_mul_bits(…))) it takes 17–19 ns. The native code of both
functions is nearly identical (168 vs 179 instructions, the same single out-of-line call).
Expected: the wrapper (an isbits struct around the UInt64) costs nothing.
Actual: about 7 ns per product in some runs. The VM’s run-to-run noise (up to about 40%)
makes it unclear how much is real: one run of the bare variant also took 18 ns.
Consequence: GF(2^64) keeps MulTable as default. Investigate on a quiet machine
(code_llvm of the whole broadcast loop, perf), then reconsider the default.

FF-P2 — CLMulMatMul is slow for matrix × vector (resolved, 2026-11-20)

Where: julia/FiniteFieldArithmetic.jl/src/bulk.jl, matmul_add!(::CLMulMatMul, …), the
default for A * x above GF(256) (below the bitsliced threshold, which a vector never reaches).
Reproduction: bench/matmul_threshold.jl, rows … × 1: 1024 \times 1024 times a vector
takes 9.0 ns per multiply-add at GF(2^32), 17.5 at GF(2^64), 70 at GF(2^128), against 0.3, 0.6
and 3 per multiply-add for square products.
Expected: about the cost of a square product per multiply-add.
Actual: the conversion of all of A to the polynomial basis (and A transposed) is paid
for one column; for a vector it costs more than the products. (An explanation from the code,
not profiled.)
Consequence: none for correctness. Options: a matrix × vector path without converting A
(scalar CLMul products, or MulBy-style tables of the vector entries), chosen by q.
Resolution (2026-11-20): a column-wise path without the transpose (clmul_columns_add!),
chosen by clmul_by_columns(F, m, p, q): a vector with A \ge 512 KiB, two columns with
A \ge 4 MiB and m, p \ge 256. The measurement showed the crossover depends on the size of
A, not only on q: for small A the transposed path is as fast or faster even for a vector.
1024 \times 1024 times a vector now 1.05 / 2.94 / 14.9 ns per multiply-add at GF(2^32) /
GF(2^64) / GF(2^128). Details and bench/matvec.jl in src/bulk.md, “Matrix × vector”.

Research/Canonical-extension-of-the-nimb.title: Canonical extension of the nimbers
Research/Canonical-extension-of-the-nimb.content:
overview characteristic-2 categorical open-problem

Research note (2026-11-21), asked by the maintainer: is there a canonical structure on all
finite fields \mathbb{F}_{2^n} that extends the nimbers, with nesting and embeddings, but no
arbitrary choices (no polynomial tables, no pseudo-random searches)? Answer: yes, Conway’s
field \mathbf{On}_2 below \omega^{\omega^\omega}. Only the \mathbb{F}_{2^{2^k}} are
initial segments there; for other n the elements are large ordinals, but numbering the
elements of \mathbb{F}_{2^n} by their rank in ordinal order gives a canonical, \mathbb{F}_2-linear,
n-bit encoding that is the nimber value when n = 2^k. R1 (below) computed all of it for
n \le 128: Lenstra’s \alpha_u for every prime u \le 127 (17 of them new) and the rank-encoding data.


Sources (read): J. DiMuro, On On_p, arXiv:1108.0962v3 (2015): Lemma 1.1, Theorem 3.1,
Lemma 3.6, Proposition 4.1, Theorem 4.3, Corollary 4.4, Theorem 4.6, Table 1 (which, per
DiMuro, first appeared in H. W. Lenstra, On the algebraic closure of two, Proc. Kon. Ned.
Akad. Wet. A 80 (1977) 389–396; that paper was not obtained). H. W. Lenstra, Nim
multiplication, IHES/M/78/211 (scan, contents skimmed only). Lean: CombinatorialGames
(github.com/vihdzp/combinatorial-games, commit dbab731), Nimber/SimplestExtension/*
(all four simplest extension theorems, after Siegel, Combinatorial Game Theory, pp. 440–444;
the nimbers are algebraically closed) and Nimber/SmallDegree/*; it has nothing on Lenstra’s
\alpha_u (searched). Wikipedia, Nimber (the smallest algebraically closed subfield is the
ordinals below \omega^{\omega^\omega}, citing Conway 1976, p. 61).
Scripts: research/nimber_closure/verify_lenstra_table.jl, gf8_as_ordinals.jl,
degree_estimates.py.

The structure of \mathbf{On}_2 below \omega^{\omega^\omega}
Conway defines nim-addition and nim-multiplication on all ordinals by the minimal-excludant
recursion (the same definition that gives our finite nimbers), and the result is an
algebraically closed field. Every choice is forced by the definition: at each step the next
field is the extension by a root of the lexicographically earliest polynomial without a root
(DiMuro §1.1; the simplest extension theorem, formalized in CombinatorialGames). So whatever
follows is canonical in exactly the sense in which the nimbers already are.
DiMuro, Theorem 3.1 (for p = 2), with \chi_r for prime powers r = u^n:
\chi_{2^n} = [2^{2^{n-1}}] (the finite nimber fields), and for the k-th odd prime u,
\chi_{u^n} = [\omega^{\omega^{k-1} u^{n-1}}], e.g. \chi_3 = \omega, \chi_9 = [\omega^3],
\chi_5 = [\omega^\omega], \chi_7 = [\omega^{\omega^2}].

[\omega^{\omega^\omega}] is the first transcendental; the ordinals below it that are fields are
exactly the \chi_r.
\chi_{u^n} is a degree-u extension of \chi_{u^{n-1}} (and closed under extensions of
degree u' < u).
For odd u: \chi_u^{\,u} = \alpha_u, the smallest ordinal in \chi_u with no u-th root
in \chi_u; and \chi_{u^{n+1}}^{\,u} = \chi_{u^n} for n \ge 1.
For u = 2: the Artin–Schreier tower of our nimbers.

number m, the excess; \chi_h for any h is a sum of \chi_r given by Theorem 4.3.

[\sum \varphi^i \alpha_i] equals the nim-expression \sum \varphi^i \alpha_i, so elements are
nested radical-extension polynomials with finite nimbers at the bottom.

Finding 2: a canonical n-bit encoding, the rank in ordinal order
By Lemma 1.1 and induction, below \omega^{\omega^\omega} every ordinal is a finite set of
“digits” (monomials \prod \chi_r^{e_r} times a power of two of the finite level), nim-addition
is the symmetric difference (XOR) of digit sets, and the ordinal order compares the highest
differing digit. \mathbb{F}_{2^n} is an n-dimensional \mathbb{F}_2-subspace. Its reduced
echelon basis b_{n-1} > \dots > b_0 (distinct leading digits, no basis vector containing
another’s leading digit) makes the map
\operatorname{rank} : \mathbb{F}_{2^n} \to \{0, \dots, 2^n - 1\},\qquad
\textstyle\sum_i \varepsilon_i b_i \mapsto \sum_i \varepsilon_i 2^i
order-preserving (the leading digits decide) and \mathbb{F}_2-linear. So: number the elements
of \mathbb{F}_{2^n} by their position in ordinal order. (Sketch of proof; the
order-preservation is the standard argument for echelon bases, to be written out properly.)

No choice is made anywhere: the ordinals, the field, and the order are Conway’s.
For n = 2^k, \mathbb{F}_{2^n} is the initial segment of ordinals below 2^n, i.e. the
integers below 2^n, and rank = value: exactly our Nimber.
\mathbb{F}_8 above: ranks 0 … 7 in the listed order; e.g. rank 2 ⊕ rank 4 = rank 6 ✓.
Embeddings \mathbb{F}_{2^m} \hookrightarrow \mathbb{F}_{2^n} for m \mid n are the
inclusions inside \mathbf{On}_2: canonical, compatible (a functor from the divisibility
poset, colimit = \omega^{\omega^\omega} itself), and in rank coordinates a fixed m \times n
bit matrix. Equality and hashing across fields can go through the ordinal (or through the
smallest subfield), as with nimbers.
Arithmetic in rank coordinates: through any internal basis (e.g. a polynomial basis with
carry-less products, as CLMul does for nimbers) and an n \times n change of basis. The
internal basis is invisible, so it is an implementation choice, not a convention of the
structure.
The runtime data per n is small (n \times n bits, plus a modulus and the embedding images);
the work is computing it once.

Categorically: this is the canonical choice of one embedding per pair m \mid n that Conway
polynomials provide by a table, here provided by \mathbf{On}_2; with rank coordinates each
\mathbb{F}_{2^n} also gets a canonical \mathbb{F}_2-basis, which Conway polynomials do not
give (they give a canonical generator).

Research/Rank-encoding-is-order-preservi.title: Rank encoding is order-preserving
Research/Rank-encoding-is-order-preservi.content:
theorem proof characteristic-2

Theorem. Let \mathbb{F}_{2^n} be the subfield of Conway’s \mathbf{On}_2 with 2^n elements
and b_0 < \dots < b_{n-1} its reduced echelon basis with respect to the ordinal order. Then
\operatorname{rank}^{-1} : k = \sum_{i \in e} 2^i \mapsto \sum_{i \in e} b_i is a strictly
increasing bijection \{0, \dots, 2^n - 1\} \to \mathbb{F}_{2^n}. So the element of rank k is the
k-th smallest element (from 0), and the rank is \mathbb{F}_2-linear: the encoding of
ADR-0005 Rank encoding of GF(2^n) in Conway’s On2 is well defined and canonical.


Sources: J. DiMuro, On On_p, arXiv:1108.0962v3, Lemma 1.1 and Theorem 3.1 (the structure of
\mathbf{On}_2 below \omega^{\omega^\omega}); see Canonical extension of the nimbers.
mathlib: Finset.Colex.toColex_lt_toColex_iff_max'_mem,
Finset.Colex.geomSum_lt_geomSum_iff_toColex_lt_toColex.
Lean (complete, no sorry, only the standard axioms): lean/FiniteFields/RankEncoding.lean
(spanSum_strictMono, spanSum_lt_of_rank_lt: step 2) and lean/FiniteFields/NimberDigits.lean
(digits_add, digits_strictMono, nimSum_lt_of_rank_lt: step 1 for binary digits, on
CombinatorialGames’ Nimber, and the theorem for nimbers).
Checked numerically: research/nimber_closure/check_rank_data.jl (check 5, all elements of 13
fields up to 2^{20} elements).

Step 1: elements below \omega^{\omega^\omega} are digit sets in colex order
Let L be a finite tower inside \mathbf{On}_2: a finite nimber field \mathbb{F}_{2^{2^a}} (the
ordinals below 2^{2^a}) and generators g_1 < \dots < g_k (each a \chi_r, DiMuro Thm 3.1),
where g_j generates a degree-u_j extension and g_j^{u_j} lies in the tower of
g_1, \dots, g_{j-1}. Every x \in L is uniquely
x = \sum_{e} g_k^{e_k} \cdots g_1^{e_1}\, c_e, \qquad 0 \le e_j < u_j,\ c_e \in \mathbb{F}_{2^{2^a}} .
Ordinal. By DiMuro’s Lemma 1.1, applied to the top generator and then inductively to the
coefficients: if \tilde\varphi = [\varphi^u] is the degree-u extension of the field \varphi by
the root \varphi, then the nim-expression \sum_{i<u} \varphi^i \alpha_i (\alpha_i < \varphi) is the
ordinal [\varphi^{u-1}\alpha_{u-1} + \dots + \alpha_0] (ordinal arithmetic). For a generator
g_j whose field below is larger than the tower g_1, \dots, g_{j-1}, the coefficients are
still ordinals below g_j, so the statement applies to elements of L unchanged.
Order. Ordinals of the form [\varphi^{u-1}\alpha_{u-1} + \dots + \alpha_0] with all
\alpha_i < \varphi are compared by the highest i with \alpha_i \ne \alpha'_i, then by
\alpha_i (the base-\varphi Cantor normal form). Inductively, two elements of L compare by
the largest monomial g_k^{e_k} \cdots g_1^{e_1} (exponent of g_k first, then g_{k-1}, …) in
which their coefficients differ, and then by those coefficients, which are finite nimbers, i.e.
integers, compared by their highest differing bit.
Digits. Call a pair (monomial, bit 2^c, c < 2^a) a digit, ordered as just described (monomial
first, then bit). Then x \mapsto (its set of digits with coefficient bit 1) identifies L with
the finite subsets of the digits, the ordinal order with the colexicographic order (compare the
largest digit in the symmetric difference), and nim-addition with the symmetric difference
(addition is coefficientwise, DiMuro’s map \theta is additive, and finite nim-addition is XOR).
Independence of the tower. A larger tower L' \supseteq L (more generators, larger base) adds
digits but keeps the relative order of the old ones, so the order of two elements does not depend
on the tower used. Hence ranks are absolute: they depend only on the subfield.
Step 2: a reduced echelon basis gives an order-preserving rank
\mathbb{F}_{2^n} \subseteq L is an n-dimensional \mathbb{F}_2-subspace of the digit sets. Gaussian
elimination with pivots at the largest digit gives the reduced echelon basis: b_0, \dots, b_{n-1}
with largest digits p_0 < \dots < p_{n-1}, and p_i \notin b_j for j \ne i. For
e \subseteq \{0, \dots, n-1\} let s(e) = \triangle_{i \in e} b_i (a digit lies in s(e) iff it lies in
an odd number of the b_i, i \in e).
Lemma (Lean: spanSum_strictMono). If e <_{\text{colex}} e' then
s(e) <_{\text{colex}} s(e').
Proof. Let i = \max(e \triangle e'); e <_{\text{colex}} e' means i \in e', so i \notin e, and above
i the sets agree. Let m = p_i.
(a) m \in s(e') and m \notin s(e): m lies in b_j only for j = i (reduced), and
i \in e', i \notin e.
(b) For a digit x > m: if x \in b_j then p_j \ge x > m = p_i, so j > i; there e and e'
agree, so x lies in the same number of b_j for e and for e': x \in s(e) \iff x \in s(e').
So every digit in s(e) \setminus s(e') is < m (not > m by (b), not m by (a)), and
m \in s(e') \setminus s(e): that is s(e) <_{\text{colex}} s(e'). \square
Since k = \sum_{i \in e} 2^i orders the e exactly as colex does (binary numbers; mathlib’s
geomSum_lt_geomSum_iff_toColex_lt_toColex), k \mapsto s(e) is strictly increasing in k
(Lean: spanSum_lt_of_rank_lt). It is onto \mathbb{F}_{2^n} (a basis spans), so it is the
increasing enumeration: the element of rank k is the k-th smallest. Linearity:
s(e \triangle e') = s(e) \triangle s(e'). \square
theorem spanSum_strictMono (b : ι → Finset α) (hne : ∀ i, (b i).Nonempty)
    (hp : StrictMono fun i => (b i).max' (hne i))
    (hred : ∀ i j, i ≠ j → (b i).max' (hne i) ∉ b j) :
    StrictMono fun e : Colex (Finset ι) => toColex (spanSum b (ofColex e))
 
theorem spanSum_lt_of_rank_lt (b : ℕ → Finset α) (hne : ∀ i, (b i).Nonempty)
    (hp : StrictMono fun i => (b i).max' (hne i))
    (hred : ∀ i j, i ≠ j → (b i).max' (hne i) ∉ b j) {e e' : Finset ℕ}
    (h : ∑ i ∈ e, 2 ^ i < ∑ i ∈ e', 2 ^ i) :
    toColex (spanSum b e) < toColex (spanSum b e')
Step 1 in Lean: binary digits instead of tower digits
The formal proof uses a simpler digit structure than the tower of step 1, valid on all
ordinals and needing no description of \mathbf{On}_2 at all: the binary Cantor normal form
o = 2^{e_1} + 2^{e_2} + \dots (e_1 > e_2 > \dots), digits o = \{e_1, e_2, \dots\}.

digits_add: nim-addition is the symmetric difference of binary digits. Proof: every nimber is
the nim-sum \sum_{e \in \text{digits}} {*}2^e (by Nimber.two_opow_log_add), and for
r < 2^m the nim-sum {*}2^m + {*}r is the ordinal 2^m + r (IsGroup.add_eq_of_lt, since
2^m is a group, IsGroup.two_opow); in characteristic 2 the common digits cancel.
digits_strictMono: the ordinal order is colex on binary digits (compare \log_2, then the
remainders, by well-founded induction).
nimSum_lt_of_rank_lt: for any nimbers b_i forming a reduced echelon family for their binary
digits, \sum_{i \in e} b_i increases strictly with \sum_{i \in e} 2^i.

So the theorem holds for every finite \mathbb{F}_2-subspace of the nimbers, in particular every
finite subfield, with “digit” meaning binary digit. The R1 computation used tower digits
(monomials times nimber bits, step 1 above); that both give the same order is DiMuro’s Lemma 1.1,
which stays the one unformalized link between the computed data and the Lean theorem (it is also
what check 5 of check_rank_data.jl tests by brute force). Not formalized either: the existence of
a reduced echelon basis (standard linear algebra).
Remarks
Comparison with \mathbb{R}, \mathbb{C}: there is no
analogue: an ordered field has no finite subfields, and here the order is not a field order
(it is compatible neither with multiplication nor with translation x \mapsto x + c); the lemma
says only that rank coordinates enumerate the subfield in increasing order.

Specifications/Prime-field-arithmetic.title: Prime field arithmetic
Specifications/Prime-field-arithmetic.content:
Status: planned. Lean reuses mathlib’s field structure (smoke test only). The Julia starter
was removed on 2026-11-19; the Julia side will be part of FiniteFieldArithmetic.jl (backlog J4),
after the characteristic-2 work.
Julia: none yet
Lean: lean/FiniteFields.lean
Decision: ADR-0002 Reuse mathlib
Scope
For a prime integer p, represent elements of the prime field with p elements and implement
construction, addition, subtraction, multiplication, additive negation, inversion, and division.
Extension fields are out of scope.
Requirements

A value constructed from an integer is reduced to its canonical residue in [0, p-1].
Construction rejects a modulus less than two or a composite modulus.
Addition, subtraction, and multiplication return the corresponding residue class.
Every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse; inversion and division by zero fail
explicitly.
Lean uses mathlib’s ZMod p and prime-field instance rather than introducing a duplicate field
definition.

Acceptance checks

Julia tests cover positive and negative reduction, arithmetic wraparound, inverse, division,
invalid moduli, and zero inverse.
lake build succeeds with the ZMod p field-instance example.

Open
Element storage width, reduction strategy (Barrett, Montgomery) and primality checking are to be
decided with J4; see AGENTS.md, Julia conventions.
